headline: Reagan sworn in as the hostages come home
text: Ronald Reagan became president on 20 January. On the same day Iran released the 52 American hostages after 444 days, under a deal signed in Algiers the day before.

headline: Reagan ends US oil price controls
text: In January the new president removed price controls on US oil. Prices will now follow the market. OPEC members have no common price and use benchmarks between 32 and 36 dollars a barrel.

headline: Exxon's profit rose 31.8 percent in 1980
text: Exxon reported in late January that its profit for 1980 rose 31.8 percent. It is the biggest company in America by sales. Dearer oil is the reason for the jump.

headline: Siemens gets a new chief
text: Karlheinz Kaske was named head of the management board of Siemens, the German electrical giant, on 28 January, succeeding Bernhard Plettner. Siemens made its first digital telephone exchange in 1980.

headline: Coup attempt in Spain fails after the king speaks out
text: On 23 February a coup was attempted in Spain by Antonio Tejero. King Juan Carlos denounced it, and it failed.

headline: General Jaruzelski becomes prime minister of Poland
text: On 9 February the Polish army general Wojciech Jaruzelski took over as prime minister. The free trade union Solidarity was founded last September.

headline: Fire at a Dublin nightclub kills 48 young people
text: A fire at the Stardust nightclub in Artane, Dublin, killed 48 young people in the early hours of 14 February. A further 214 were injured, so 262 people were killed or hurt in a single night.

headline: Reagan asks Congress for deep tax and spending cuts
text: On 18 February Reagan asked Congress to cut income tax rates by 10 percent a year for three years and to cut 41.4 billion dollars from federal spending in 1982. He pointed to almost 8 million Americans out of work, double-digit inflation for two years running, and interest rates above 20 percent.

headline: Buffett: Berkshire's book value per share up to 400.80 dollars
text: In his letter to shareholders, dated 27 February, Warren Buffett reports operating earnings of 41.9 million dollars for 1980, up from 36.0, and book value per share of 400.80 against 335.85 a year earlier. Berkshire now owns 7.2 million shares of GEICO, about a third of it, for 47 million dollars. The textile business lost money.

headline: Roberto Goizueta takes over at Coca-Cola
text: Roberto Goizueta became Coca-Cola's chairman in March, succeeding Paul Austin. Goizueta joined Coca-Cola's bottler in Cuba in 1954 and left for the United States after Castro's rise. He was made president in 1979.

headline: President Reagan shot in the chest
text: John Hinckley fired at President Reagan on 30 March, only ten weeks after he took office. Reagan was hit in the chest and wounded. His press secretary James Brady and two policemen were hurt too.

headline: Walter Cronkite signs off the CBS Evening News
text: After 19 years as host, Walter Cronkite read the evening news for the last time on 6 March, ending as always with "And that's the way it is". Often called "the most trusted man in America", he left because CBS made anchors retire at 65. Dan Rather took over the following Monday.

headline: Daimler-Benz, the maker of Mercedes, is now available to you
text: Daimler-Benz, the German company behind Mercedes cars and lorries, has long been listed in Germany; you can now buy it too. The G-Class off-roader and the new S-Class, its flagship, both arrived in September 1979. Gerhard Prinz has been chairman since 1980.

headline: BMW, the maker of sporty cars, is now available to you
text: BMW has long been listed in Germany; you can now buy it too. It sold 339,232 cars in 1980, up from 335,132, with the 3 Series (1975), the 5 Series (1972) and the M1 sports car (1978). The Quandt family's investment in 1959 saved it from bankruptcy. It is smaller than Mercedes but is known for sporty cars.

headline: Jack Welch takes charge at General Electric
text: Jack Welch took over as chairman and chief executive of General Electric in April. GE had 411,000 employees at the end of 1980 and is worth about 12 to 14 billion dollars on the stock market. At 45 he is its youngest chairman ever.

headline: Exxon tops the Fortune 500 with sales of 103 billion dollars
text: Fortune's list of the biggest industrial firms, out on 16 April, puts Exxon first again with 103.14 billion dollars of sales, the first company ever over 100 billion. Mobil is second ahead of General Motors, and oil companies hold 13 of the top 20 places.

headline: Space Shuttle Columbia flies
text: Columbia lifted off on 12 April on its first mission and came back two days later. It is the first reusable crewed spacecraft.

headline: Dow reaches 1,024 as hopes for Reagan's plans run high
text: The Dow Jones average climbed to 1,024 in April, 12 percent above its December low, on hopes for Reagan's tax cuts. Yet interest rates are still very high.

headline: Riots in Brixton, London
text: Riots shook Brixton in south London from 10 to 12 April, and hundreds of people were hurt, most of them police officers. Over 100 vehicles and about 30 buildings were burned. Police had stopped and searched 943 people in the five days before, and unemployment among young black people was very high.

headline: Sandoz sales rise 10% to 4.9 billion francs, but Basel lags
text: On 30 April Sandoz reported 1980 sales up 10.3% to 4.9 billion Swiss francs and group profit up 16.8% to 202 million. The dividend stays at 65 francs a share. Drugs, about half of sales, grew faster in the second half, while dyes weakened as the textile industry slowed. The Basel parent company is a worry: its own sales fell 3%.

headline: France elects a Socialist president
text: Francois Mitterrand took office as president of France on 21 May, the first Socialist president of the Fifth Republic. He had beaten Valery Giscard d'Estaing by 51.76 percent to 48.24 percent on 10 May, helped by Communist voters, about a fifth of the electorate. His programme was called the 110 Propositions for France.

headline: Pope John Paul II shot in St. Peter's Square
text: A Turkish gunman, Mehmet Ali Agca, shot Pope John Paul II on 13 May in St. Peter's Square in Rome. Two bullets hit the Pope, who lost a lot of blood and had emergency surgery, and two bystanders from the US were also wounded. Vatican security, a nun and spectators held Agca, who had escaped from a Turkish military prison in 1979 after confessing to killing a newspaper editor.

headline: Bob Marley dies at 36
text: The reggae singer Bob Marley died of cancer on 11 May in Miami, aged 36, on the way home to Jamaica from a clinic in Germany. In February Jamaica had given him its Order of Merit, and it held a state funeral for him on 21 May.

headline: WHO adopts a code on baby milk, Nestle under pressure
text: On 21 May the World Health Organization voted 118 to 1 for an international code on how to sell milk powder for babies. Since 1977 critics have boycotted Nestle, charging that its aggressive marketing in poor countries discourages mothers from breastfeeding.

headline: Doctors report a strange pneumonia in young men in Los Angeles
text: On 5 June the US Centers for Disease Control reported five cases of a rare pneumonia in gay men in Los Angeles. Doctors are still looking for the cause.

headline: The Fed's key rate hits 20 percent
text: The rate banks charge each other, which the Federal Reserve steers, has climbed from about 11 percent in 1979 to 20 percent by June. Fed chairman Paul Volcker is using high rates to squeeze inflation out of the economy, and borrowing has rarely been so expensive.

headline: Baseball players go on strike in mid-season
text: Major league baseball players walked out on 12 June, in the middle of the season, and part of the season has already been cancelled. The fight is over what a team should get when it loses a free agent, a player free to sign with anyone, to another team.

headline: Israel bombs Iraq's nuclear reactor
text: On 7 June Israeli aircraft destroyed the Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad, which Iraq had bought from France. Eight F-16s with F-15 escorts flew over 1,600 km, and Israel said the reactor was less than a month from starting up. The UN Security Council condemned the raid, with US support, and the US suspended delivery of four F-16s to Israel.

headline: Congress votes for Reagan's big tax cut
text: On 29 July the House of Representatives voted 323 to 107 for Reagan's tax plan; the Senate approved it by voice vote on the 31st. The top rate of income tax falls from 70 to 50 percent, and the cuts for individuals come in steps over three years.

headline: Disney's The Fox and the Hound opens
text: Disney released the cartoon The Fox and the Hound on 10 July. It is the last film worked on by the veteran animators known as the Nine Old Men. Meanwhile Disney is building EPCOT Center, a new park, in Florida.

headline: Nintendo launches Donkey Kong
text: Nintendo of Japan released the arcade game Donkey Kong on 9 July. Its hero, a carpenter, has to save a woman from a giant ape.

headline: Walkway collapses in a Kansas City hotel, more than 100 dead
text: A walkway collapsed at the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City on 17 July, killing more than 100 people. It happened on a Friday evening at a tea dance, with about 1,600 people in the lobby of a hotel that had opened only a year earlier. The fourth-floor walkway fell onto the one below, and both crashed to the floor.

headline: MTV goes on air
text: The cable channel MTV began at 12:01 on the morning of 1 August with the song Video Killed the Radio Star. Owned by Warner-Amex, it opened with footage of the Apollo 11 Moon landing, in which the flag turned into the MTV logo. It shows music videos introduced by video jockeys.

headline: Air traffic controllers strike and Reagan fires them
text: The controllers' union struck on 3 August, asking for a 32-hour week and 600 million dollars of raises over three years. Reagan ordered them back within 48 hours, and on 5 August he fired more than 11,000 who had stayed out, banning them from federal jobs for life. Striking was illegal for government workers.

headline: IBM launches a personal computer for 1,565 dollars
text: IBM presented its Personal Computer on 12 August. The base model costs 1,565 dollars with 16 KB of memory, and runs a system from Microsoft. A small team in Boca Raton, Florida, built it in a year from standard parts, unlike IBM's usual in-house way.

headline: The brain of IBM's PC is an Intel chip
text: IBM chose Intel's 8088 processor, running at 4.77 MHz, for its new PC. For Intel, which has been under pressure from cheap memory chips, it is a big customer for its microprocessors.

headline: Reagan signs the biggest tax cut in US history
text: Reagan signed the Economic Recovery Tax Act on 13 August. It cuts the top tax rate from 70 to 50 percent and the lowest from 14 to 11, and lets businesses write off equipment faster.

headline: Sony shows a camera that has no film
text: On 25 August Sony showed a prototype of the Mavica. It records still pictures as video signals onto small magnetic disks, 50 pictures to a disk. It is a prototype, and Sony has not said when one might go on sale.

headline: Apple welcomes IBM to the computer market in a newspaper ad
text: Apple bought a full page in the Wall Street Journal with the headline Welcome, IBM. Seriously. Its own sales in the first half of 1981 already beat all of 1980, which were 118 million dollars. Most Apple IIs go to businesses, not to hobbyists.

headline: Boeing's new 767 makes its first flight
text: The Boeing 767 flew for the first time on 26 September. United Airlines ordered 30 in 1978 to launch it. It has two engines and is the first Boeing wide-body with a cockpit designed for two pilots, with computer screens.

headline: Mercedes adds a two-door coupe to the S-Class
text: Daimler-Benz showed the SEC coupe, a two-door version of the S-Class, at the Frankfurt motor show in September, as the 380 SEC and 500 SEC, both with V8 engines. It has no B-pillar and a world-first seat-belt presenter that moves the belt forward to the driver. It goes with the sedans launched in 1979.

headline: Sandra Day O'Connor takes her seat as first woman on the Supreme Court
text: Sandra Day O'Connor was sworn in on 25 September as the first woman ever to sit on the US Supreme Court. Reagan had promised in his 1980 campaign to name a woman. The Senate confirmed her 99 to 0 on 21 September; in Arizona she had been the first woman to lead a state senate as majority leader.

headline: France opens a high-speed train between Paris and Lyon
text: The TGV, France's new high-speed train, began service between Paris and Lyon on 27 September. The French railways had ordered 87 of the trains from Alstom in 1976. They charged the same ticket price as on the slower line next to it, so fast travel was meant for everyone.

headline: America's doctors' association sells its tobacco shares
text: The American Medical Association sold about 1.4 million dollars of tobacco shares, including R.J. Reynolds and Philip Morris, from its pension fund. Students and young doctors had called it hypocritical for a medical group to own cigarette makers. A spokeswoman admitted the holdings had hurt its campaign against smoking.

headline: Egypt's President Sadat shot dead at a parade
text: Egypt's President Anwar Sadat was assassinated on 6 October during a military parade in Cairo. Hosni Mubarak was elected to succeed him on the 14th.

headline: OPEC agrees on 32 dollars as Saudi Arabia pumps more oil
text: Saudi Arabia, which has been pumping more oil to win back customers, forced the other members to cut prices. By October OPEC settled on a 32 dollar benchmark price, though members adjust it by quality.

headline: McDonald's game: two women claim the 300,000 dollar grand prize
text: McDonald's is running a 15 million dollar prize game in which the top prize is 300,000 dollars, at odds of one in 416,670,000. Judy Heitkamp, 24, was named the winner after she sent in a stamp on 15 October. A woman in Berkeley says she held the same winning stamp weeks earlier, lost it to a coworker, and has complained to the police.

headline: Helmut Maucher becomes chief executive of Nestle
text: Helmut Maucher, a German, became chief executive of Nestle in November. He came to the Swiss headquarters last year as general director after running the group's German business. He takes over a food group under fire for how it sells baby milk in poor countries.

headline: Luke and Laura marry on General Hospital
text: The wedding of Luke and Laura on the soap General Hospital on 16 November was the highest-rated hour in the history of American soaps, with 30 million viewers. Elizabeth Taylor, who had phoned the studio herself, appeared as Helena Cassadine.

headline: US and Soviet talks on missiles in Europe begin in Geneva
text: On 30 November American and Soviet negotiators began talks in Geneva on cutting medium-range nuclear weapons in Europe. NATO had decided in 1979 to deploy new American missiles, due from 1983, unless talks worked. On 18 November Reagan had offered his "zero option": no new missiles if the Soviets scrapped their SS-4, SS-5 and SS-20 missiles.

headline: Poland's army declares martial law
text: On 13 December General Jaruzelski declared martial law in Poland to crush Solidarity. Phone lines were cut, a curfew began, the borders were sealed, and Solidarity members were arrested overnight. On 16 December nine miners were shot dead at the Wujek mine.

headline: Dow ends 1981 at 875, down 9 percent
text: The Dow Jones average closed the year at 875.00, a drop of 9.2 percent from 963.99 a year earlier. High interest rates have hurt shares.

headline: First American test-tube baby is born
text: Elizabeth Jordan Carr was born in Norfolk, Virginia, on 28 December, the first American baby conceived outside the womb. She weighed 5 pounds 12 ounces and was the 15th baby in the world born this way, after Louise Brown in Britain in 1978. Drs Howard and Georgeanna Jones at Eastern Virginia Medical School helped her mother, who had lost her fallopian tubes, to conceive.

headline: Wal-Mart moves into the Southeast and takes over Big K
text: Wal-Mart expanded into the Southeast in 1981, opening stores in Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina. In June it agreed to take over Kuhn's Big K, a struggling rival, in a deal valued at 13 million dollars, adding 92 stores. The little chain from Arkansas is becoming a regional power.

headline: Jack Welch: every GE business must be first or second in its market
text: In a speech in New York on 8 December, GE's new chairman Jack Welch said GE should keep only businesses that are number one or number two in their markets. The others are to go. For a company that makes everything from light bulbs to jet engines, that means big changes and job cuts.
